transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um, well, the main reason I’m here is that when I'm on the floor at work—I'm a registered nurse—I just lose my train of thought constantly. Like, an IV pump will beep, or someone will ask another nurse a question... which happens all the time, especially with the new grads. We had this one girl start last week who didn't even know where the main supply closet was after three days, and I get that orientation is super rushed right now because our unit is chronically short-staffed, but it's just a lot to deal with when you're trying to chart. But anyway, yeah, someone asks a question or a call light goes off down the hall, and suddenly I’ve completely forgotten what patient flow issue I was even working on. It just completely leaves my brain.
Have you struggled with focus and distractibility like this throughout your life, or is this something that started more recently?

Oh, it's definitely been my whole life. Like, even back in elementary school, my teachers were always writing on my report cards that I was, you know, 'bright but careless.' I was constantly losing my worksheets or just completely forgetting to turn in my homework. I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was so strict, she used to make us use these specific color-coded folders for every single subject. Red for math, blue for reading. I actually still try to use color-coding at work now with my highlighters, but then another nurse always borrows my pink highlighter and never gives it back. It drives me crazy because I buy the nice pastel ones from Target, not the cheap neon ones the hospital supplies, and they aren't cheap. 

But anyway, what was I... right, school. Yeah, I was always losing those worksheets. My mom actually had to sit with me at the kitchen table every single night just to keep me on track so I'd actually finish anything. She was a saint for doing that, honestly, especially since she was working second shift back then and was probably exhausted. She still complains about her sleep schedule, actually... but yeah, it's definitely not a new thing for me.
Aside from feeling distracted, do you find yourself struggling with constant or excessive worry about everyday things?

Um, worry? No, not really. I mean, I don't think I worry any more than the next person. Obviously, I worry about my patients, but that's just being a good nurse. Like yesterday, I had this guy in room 412 who was just not looking right—his color was off, and his pressure was trending down, and I kept telling the resident, 'Hey, you need to come look at him,' but they were stuck in the ER with a trauma. The ER is always a mess on Tuesdays, I swear. It's like everyone decides to come in for the most random things. My friend Sarah works down there, and she was telling me about this lady who came in because she swallowed a fake fingernail. Like, how do you even do that? They were those really long acrylic ones with the rhinestones, too. I used to get my nails done like that for special occasions, but you can't have them in healthcare because of infection control. They harbor so much bacteria. Our manager is super strict about it—she actually sent a girl home last month for having gel polish on. But anyway, no, I wouldn't say I have excessive worry about everyday stuff. Just the normal things.
Do you often feel physically restless, fidgety, or like you have an inner motor running that makes it hard to sit still?

Restless? Um, no, not physically. I don't feel like I have a motor running or anything like that. I actually don't really have a problem sitting still. The problem is just that when I *am* sitting still, like at the nurses' station trying to do my charting, my brain is just... everywhere else. But physically, no. I mean, my feet hurt all the time, but that's just from being on them for twelve hours straight. I bought those expensive compression socks everyone raves about, the ones with the fun patterns? I got a pair with little coffee cups on them, which is ironic because I'm trying to cut back on caffeine. My dentist said it's staining my teeth, and I just paid for this whitening treatment that cost a fortune. It made my teeth so sensitive for like three days, I could barely drink ice water. And the ice machine on our unit has been broken for a week anyway, so we've been having to go down to the third floor just to get ice for the patients. The third-floor nurses always give us dirty looks when we do it, too, like we're stealing their ice. It's hospital ice! But yeah, no, I don't feel fidgety or anything.
